audience.programmeDescription: VU’s Media, Kunst, Design en Architectuur studies the history and theory of visual and material culture across four connected fields. A shared foundation leads to a Media, Art, Design or Architecture specialisation, open study, a research seminar and a thesis.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The UCR options emphasize media and film or art history and material culture. VU combines all four fields in its foundation and provides specialist media and art research seminars. Both UCR options have less depth in design and architecture.

curriculum.limitation: The 180 EC plan includes a study trip, 30 EC of approved open study and a 12 EC thesis with colloquium. Dutch language testing, attendance and progression requirements apply.

componentNotes.y1-skills: The Dutch language test or required refresher must be completed before the grade is released.
componentNotes.y2-studytrip: This route requires a study trip in Media and Design.
componentNotes.y3-elective: Open study can include a minor, approved individual courses, study abroad or a 12 EC internship with 18 EC of courses.
componentNotes.y3-seminar: The current seminar examines AI, data and infrastructure through media research.
componentNotes.y3-thesis: The 12 EC includes the colloquium. Entry requires passing all first- and second-year courses.

ACCPPDE101.text: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.

Students relate artists, styles and movements to social, religious, political and cultural change. MCCHEAM316.text: This course examines the history of art history as an academic discipline, tracing how scholars have understood and interpreted art from the sixteenth century to the present. Through critical readings of influential texts by figures such as Aby Warburg, Erwin Panofsky, Ernst Gombrich, Michel Foucault, and Jacques Derrida, students explore the major ideas and methodologies that have shaped the field. Topics include art and history, aesthetics, meaning and interpretation, authorship and identity, and the challenges of art history in a globalized world.

MCCHEAM315.text:
In the modern world democracy is associated with participation, rationality and freedom. In this course, we go back to the roots of democracy in ancient Greece, when to a modern observer, it was not very democratic at all: foreigners, slaves and women were excluded from elections and political decision-making. Even so, the inclusion of all classes, also the poor, in politics was after antiquity not achieved until the mid-nineteenth century.


Ancient commentators criticised Athenian democracy for being too extreme just because of this broad inclusion. They argued that many were too uneducated, too emotional, and too irrational to see through the cheap play on emotions by demagogues and would-be tyrants.


This course investigates how Athenian democracy was built, how it was intertwined with myth and religion, and expressed in art, literature and architecture. It traces the loci of democracy in archaeology, and analyses its temporary collapse in the crisis of the late fifth century BC. Most importantly, we put ourselves in our socio-political ancestors’ shoes by engaging in a simulation of the Athenian assembly, in which we have to make decisions that will change our lives forever. In doing so, we use the ancient heritage of democracy for an experiment in applied sociology – to not only understand, but to feel the meaning of political decision-making.
